doctrines.name: God and the Trinity
doctrines.question: How can the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit each be worshipped as God if God is one?
doctrines.summary: Early Christians inherited Israel's confession that God is one (the Shema) yet prayed to Jesus as Lord and baptised in the name of Father, Son and Spirit. Three centuries of argument — monarchian, Logos, Arian, homoiousian and Nicene answers — produced the creeds of Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381): one divine essence (ousia) in three persons (hypostases). The doctrine was then refined (Augustine, Aquinas, Palamas), divided East and West over the Filioque, challenged by Socinians, Unitarians and Oneness Pentecostals, and re-opened in modern debates over social versus classical Trinitarianism, divine simplicity, open theism and process theology.
doctrines.longText:
The problem is older than the word ‘Trinity’. The first Christians were Jews who recited ‘Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God is one LORD’ (Deuteronomy 6:4), yet within a generation of the crucifixion they sang hymns to Christ ‘as to a god’ (Pliny, Letter 10.96), applied to Jesus texts that Isaiah applied to YHWH (Philippians 2:10–11; Isaiah 45:23), and baptised ‘in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost’ (Matthew 28:19). The New Testament does not offer a technical formula; it offers a pattern of worship and a set of texts pulling in different directions — ‘I and my Father are one’ (John 10:30) beside ‘my Father is greater than I’ (John 14:28).

The second- and third-century answers fell into three families. Logos theologians (Justin, Irenaeus, Tertullian, Origen) used the Johannine and Stoic-Platonic idea of the Word to describe a Son who is truly divine yet distinct, often in ranked or ‘economic’ terms; Tertullian coined Latin trinitas and the formula one substance, three persons. Monarchians, anxious to protect the single rule (monarchia) of God, either made Jesus a man uniquely empowered by God (dynamic monarchianism: Theodotus, Paul of Samosata) or made Father, Son and Spirit successive modes of the one God (modalism: Noetus, Praxeas, Sabellius). Both were rejected by most bishops, but the Logos tradition left an unresolved question: is the Son ‘second’ God by nature, or only in order?

Arius of Alexandria (c. 318) pressed the subordinationist logic to its conclusion: the Son is the first and greatest creature, ‘there was when he was not’. The Council of Nicaea (325) answered with the non-biblical word homoousios — ‘of the same essence’ as the Father. Far from ending the debate, Nicaea opened sixty years of conflict involving emperors, exiles and rival councils: Homoians (‘like the Father according to the Scriptures’), Heteroousians or Anomoeans (‘unlike in essence’), and Homoiousians (‘like in essence’), the last of whom Athanasius and the Cappadocians eventually won to the Nicene side. Basil of Caesarea, Gregory of Nazianzus and Gregory of Nyssa distinguished ousia (what God is) from hypostasis (who the Father, Son and Spirit are), and Basil defended the Spirit's equal glory. The Council of Constantinople (381) expanded the creed to confess the Spirit ‘the Lord and Giver of life, who proceeds from the Father, who with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified’. That Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed remains the one creed shared by Eastern Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox, the Church of the East, Catholics, and most Protestants.

After 381 the paths diverged in emphasis. Augustine's De Trinitate explored analogies in the human mind and spoke of the Spirit as the mutual love of Father and Son, supporting the Western addition that the Spirit proceeds ‘and from the Son’ (Filioque), inserted at Toledo (589) and later adopted at Rome (c. 1014). Photius (867) objected that it confused the persons and was unilaterally added to an ecumenical creed; the Filioque became a standing grievance at the Great Schism (1054) and the failed reunion councils of Lyon (1274) and Florence (1439). Medieval scholastics (Aquinas) framed the persons as subsisting relations within an absolutely simple God; Gregory Palamas distinguished God's unknowable essence from his uncreated energies.

The Reformation churches confessed the Nicene faith, but the Radical Reformation produced anti-Trinitarians: Michael Servetus was burned at Geneva (1553); the Socinians of Poland issued the Racovian Catechism (1605); Unitarian churches grew in Transylvania (from 1568), England and New England (Channing, 1819). In 1913–16 the Oneness or ‘Jesus' Name’ movement split from early Pentecostalism, teaching one God manifested as Father, Son and Spirit — today a large global movement especially in Latin America, Africa and Asia. All of these stand outside historic Nicene orthodoxy and are described here in their own terms.

The twentieth century saw a ‘Trinitarian revival’ (Barth, Rahner, Zizioulas, Moltmann). Social Trinitarians stress three persons in loving communion as a model for church and society; classical Trinitarians reply that this risks tritheism and recover Nicene and scholastic teaching on divine simplicity. Open theists and process theologians, from different starting points, question classical attributes such as immutability, impassibility and exhaustive foreknowledge. The Trinity therefore remains the shared grammar of most Christians and a live field of debate.

nodes.label: How can Father, Son and Spirit each be God if God is one?
nodes.text: Jewish monotheism plus the worship of Jesus and baptism in a threefold name created the problem every later position tries to solve.

nodes.label: Deut 6:4 — ‘The LORD our God is one LORD’
nodes.text: The Shema: the bedrock of Jewish and Christian monotheism. Every side claimed to protect it. Isaiah 44:6 and 45:5 reinforce it.

nodes.label: Prov 8:22 — ‘The LORD possessed (LXX: created) me’
nodes.text: Wisdom speaking. Read Christologically by all sides; the Septuagint's ‘created me’ became the Arian proof-text, which Athanasius read of the incarnate Son.

nodes.label: Phil 2:5–11 — ‘in the form of God… equal with God’
nodes.text: An early hymn: Christ in the form of God empties himself and receives the name above every name, echoing Isaiah 45:23. Cited for Christ's full deity and for kenosis.

nodes.label: Col 1:15 / John 14:28 — ‘firstborn of all creation’; ‘my Father is greater’
nodes.text: Texts used to argue the Son's subordination or creaturehood; Nicenes read them of rank in the incarnation or of the Son's eternal origin from the Father.

nodes.label: Matt 28:19 — ‘in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost’
nodes.text: The baptismal formula: one ‘name’, three named. Basic to Trinitarian worship; Oneness Pentecostals read the one name as ‘Jesus’ (Acts 2:38).

nodes.label: John 1:1–18; 10:30 — ‘the Word was God’; ‘I and my Father are one’
nodes.text: The Logos who was with God and was God, became flesh. The main source for Logos theology and Nicene doctrine.

nodes.label: John 15:26 — ‘the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father’
nodes.text: The procession text at the heart of the Filioque dispute, read alongside John 16:14–15 and Galatians 4:6 (‘the Spirit of his Son’).

nodes.label: Justin Martyr: the Logos as ‘another God’ in number
nodes.text: Christians worship the Father, the Son ‘in the second place’ and the prophetic Spirit ‘in the third’ — a ranked but genuine triad.

nodes.label: Irenaeus: the Son and Spirit as God's ‘two hands’
nodes.text: Against Gnostic intermediaries, Irenaeus insists the Creator acts directly through his own Word and Wisdom.

nodes.label: Dynamic monarchianism (adoptionist)
nodes.text: Theodotus the Cobbler at Rome (c. 190), later Paul of Samosata: Jesus is a man indwelt by divine power.

nodes.label: Modalism (Noetus, Praxeas, Sabellius)
nodes.text: One God appears successively as Father, Son and Spirit; opponents called it ‘Patripassianism’ (the Father suffered).

nodes.label: Tertullian: ‘trinitas’, one substance, three persons
nodes.text: Against Praxeas coins the Latin vocabulary the West will use for the next millennium.

nodes.label: Origen: eternal generation, three hypostases
nodes.text: The Son is eternally begotten — there was no time when he was not — yet ranked below the Father. Both Arians and Nicenes later claimed him.

nodes.label: Synod of Antioch deposes Paul of Samosata
nodes.text: Bishops condemn Paul's adoptionism; the synod reportedly also rejected ‘homoousios’ in his sense — later an embarrassment for the Nicenes.

nodes.label: Arius: the Son is the first creature
nodes.text: ‘There was when he was not.’ The Son is divine by grace, created before time, mutable in principle.

nodes.label: Council of Nicaea: homoousios
nodes.text: About 250–318 bishops, convened by Constantine, confess the Son ‘of the essence of the Father… of one substance (homoousios)’ and anathematise Arian slogans.

nodes.label: Athanasius: only God can deify; the Father is eternally Father
nodes.text: Five times exiled, Athanasius argues that a creature cannot unite us to God and that Christians already worship the Son — so he must be true God.

nodes.label: Homoiousians: ‘like in essence’
nodes.text: Basil of Ancyra's party: anti-Arian but wary of ‘homoousios’ as Sabellian. Later reconciled to Nicaea.

nodes.label: Ariminum & Seleucia: Homoian creed imposed
nodes.text: Under Constantius II, councils adopt ‘like the Father according to the Scriptures’, banning ousia-language. Jerome later wrote that the world woke to find itself Arian.

nodes.label: Pneumatomachians: the Spirit is not God
nodes.text: Some who accepted the Son's deity denied the Spirit's — the next battle line.

nodes.label: Basil, On the Holy Spirit: equal glory in worship
nodes.text: Liturgy shapes doctrine: if the Spirit is glorified ‘with’ the Father and Son, he shares their nature.

nodes.label: Cappadocians: one ousia, three hypostases
nodes.text: Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus and Gregory of Nyssa distinguish common essence from distinct persons marked by unbegottenness, begottenness and procession.

nodes.label: Council of Constantinople: the Spirit ‘worshipped and glorified’
nodes.text: Ratifies Nicaea, condemns Eunomians, Pneumatomachians, Apollinarians; produces the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed.

nodes.label: Imperial enforcement; Homoian faith survives among Goths and Vandals
nodes.text: Theodosius I enforces Nicene faith (Edict of Thessalonica, 380). Ulfilas' Homoian Christianity spreads to Goths, Vandals and Lombards; Vandal kings persecute Nicene Christians in North Africa (484).

nodes.label: Augustine, De Trinitate: the Spirit as mutual love
nodes.text: Psychological analogies (memory, understanding, will; lover, beloved, love) and the Spirit as the bond of Father and Son.

nodes.label: Third Council of Toledo adds ‘Filioque’
nodes.text: As Visigothic Spain converts from Arianism, the creed says the Spirit proceeds from the Father ‘and the Son’ to stress the Son's full deity.

nodes.label: Photius: the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone
nodes.text: The Father is the sole cause (aitia) in the Trinity; the Filioque confuses personal properties and was added without an ecumenical council.

nodes.label: Great Schism: Filioque among the charges
nodes.text: Rome had sung the Filioque since c. 1014; the mutual excommunications of 1054 cite it among other grievances.

nodes.label: Aquinas: persons as subsisting relations in a simple God
nodes.text: Scholastic synthesis: God is pure act, without parts; the persons are distinguished only by relations of origin.

nodes.label: Council of Florence: union declared, then rejected
nodes.text: Latins and Greeks agree ‘from the Father through the Son’ may mean the same as ‘and the Son’; the union is repudiated in the East.

nodes.label: Antitrinitarians: Servetus, Socinians, Unitarians
nodes.text: Servetus burned at Geneva (1553); Racovian Catechism (1605); Transylvanian Unitarian church (1568); Channing's ‘Unitarian Christianity’ (1819).

nodes.label: Oneness Pentecostalism: one God, Jesus' name
nodes.text: From the Arroyo Seco camp meeting (1913): Father, Son and Spirit are manifestations of one God, whose name is Jesus.

nodes.label: Assemblies of God affirms the Trinity
nodes.text: The Statement of Fundamental Truths forces out about a quarter of ministers, who form Oneness bodies (later the UPCI, 1945).

nodes.label: Process theology: God in becoming
nodes.text: Whitehead's Process and Reality (1929), Hartshorne, Cobb: God is dipolar, persuasive not coercive, affected by the world.

nodes.label: Barth and Rahner: Trinitarian revival
nodes.text: Barth puts the Trinity at the start of dogmatics (1932); Rahner's ‘Rule’: the economic Trinity is the immanent Trinity.

nodes.label: Social Trinitarianism
nodes.text: Moltmann, Zizioulas, Boff, Plantinga: three persons in loving communion (perichoresis) as the model for church and society.

nodes.label: Open theism
nodes.text: Pinnock et al.: God genuinely responds; the future is partly open, even to God.

nodes.label: Classical theism retrieval: simplicity and impassibility
nodes.text: Critics argue social, open and process views abandon the Nicene doctrine of God; a renewed classical theism defends simplicity, immutability and eternal generation.

nodes.label: Filioque dialogue: clarifications, no full resolution
nodes.text: Vatican clarification (1995); North American Orthodox–Catholic agreed statement (2003) urges Rome to use the original Greek creed. Many Anglican bodies omit the Filioque in ecumenical settings.

nodes.label: Today: Nicene faith confessed by most; nontrinitarian minorities
nodes.text: Eastern and Oriental Orthodox, the Church of the East, Catholics and nearly all Protestants confess the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed. Outside historic Nicene orthodoxy: Oneness Pentecostals (often estimated in the tens of millions), Latter-day Saints, Jehovah's Witnesses, Unitarians, Iglesia ni Cristo.

positions.name: Dynamic monarchianism
positions.oneLine: God is one person; Jesus was a man uniquely empowered (dynamis) by God's Spirit or Word, and in that sense adopted as Son.
coreClaims: The ‘monarchy’ (single rule) of God admits no second divine person.
Jesus was a real human being, born of the Virgin, upon whom the divine power or Word came (often at baptism).
Jesus' divinity is a matter of moral union and divine indwelling, not of nature.
The Word (Logos) is an impersonal attribute or power of God, not a distinct hypostasis.
positions.origin: Theodotus the Cobbler, a leather-merchant from Byzantium, taught it at Rome c. 190 and was excommunicated by Bishop Victor; Theodotus the Banker and Artemon continued it. Paul of Samosata, bishop of Antioch, gave it its best-known form and was deposed by a synod in 268.
proponentsOther: Photinus of Sirmium (4th c., similar views)
strongestArguments: It preserves strict biblical monotheism without philosophical distinctions of essence and person.
Early sermons in Acts speak of Jesus as ‘a man approved of God’ whom God ‘made… both Lord and Christ’ — language that sounds like exaltation rather than pre-existence.
It takes Jesus' full humanity, growth, prayer and temptation with complete seriousness.
Its adherents claimed it was the original Roman teaching before Bishop Zephyrinus (per Eusebius, HE 5.28).
strongestObjections: It cannot account for texts of pre-existence and creation through the Son (John 1:1–3; Colossians 1:16; Hebrews 1:2; Philippians 2:6).
It makes the worship of Jesus — already present in the New Testament and in Pliny's report (c. 112) — a worship of a creature.
Salvation as union with God requires that God himself, not a God-inspired man, enter human life (Irenaeus, Athanasius).
The Roman church's own leaders rejected the claim that it was original teaching, and it lost every synod it faced.
responses: Adherents read pre-existence texts as God's plan or Wisdom existing ideally before Christ's birth, not as a personal pre-existence.
They argued that the honour paid to Jesus is honour to the God who exalted him (Philippians 2:9–11).
Later Unitarians and some modern biblical scholars revived the argument that ‘high Christology’ developed after the earliest preaching.
consequences: The deposition of Paul of Samosata (268) was an early episcopal judgement on a doctrinal question; when Paul refused to vacate the church building, Christians appealed to Emperor Aurelian.
Its rejection pushed mainstream theology towards Logos theology and, eventually, Nicaea.
Its themes re-emerged in Socinianism, Unitarianism and some liberal Christologies.

positions.name: Modalism (Sabellianism)
positions.oneLine: There is one God who reveals himself in successive modes or roles — as Father in creation and law, as Son in redemption, as Spirit in sanctification.
coreClaims: God is a single person (prosopon) with three names or modes of activity.
Jesus is fully God, because he is the one God himself incarnate.
‘Father’ and ‘Son’ describe God in different relations or at different times, not eternally distinct persons.
(In some forms) the Father himself suffered in the incarnate Son — hence the opponents' label ‘Patripassian’.
positions.origin: Taught at Rome c. 190–215 by Noetus of Smyrna and Praxeas, and systematised by Sabellius (fl. c. 215), who was excommunicated by Pope Callistus. Combated by Hippolytus (Against Noetus) and Tertullian (Against Praxeas).
proponentsOther: Marcellus of Ancyra (accused of similar views, 4th c.)
strongestArguments: It affirms both strict monotheism and the full deity of Christ, which many ordinary believers held together without technical vocabulary.
Jesus says ‘he that hath seen me hath seen the Father’ (John 14:9) and is called ‘the everlasting Father’ (Isaiah 9:6).
It avoids what modalists saw as the ‘two gods’ (ditheism) of Logos theologians.
It made it plain that the God of the Old Testament himself — not a lesser being — came to save.
strongestObjections: The Gospels show the Son praying to the Father, being sent by him, and the Spirit descending at the baptism — real I–Thou relations (Matthew 3:16–17; John 17).
If the Father became the Son, the Son's revelation of the Father is a revelation of no one beyond himself, and the Son's obedience becomes play-acting.
‘Patripassianism’ attributes suffering to the Father in a way most early theologians thought unworthy of God.
Tertullian: it ‘put to flight the Paraclete, and crucified the Father’.
responses: Modalists answered that prayer and sending reflect the incarnate humanity relating to the divine, not two divine persons.
Later Oneness Pentecostals argue the distinctions are between God's deity and Christ's humanity, not between eternal persons, and that ‘person’ is post-biblical vocabulary.
Some modern theologians (e.g. Barth's ‘modes of being’) have been accused of modalism while denying it, showing the line is subtle.
consequences: Provoked Tertullian's formula ‘one substance, three persons’ and Hippolytus' polemic.
‘Sabellian’ became the standard Eastern charge against homoousios in the fourth century, slowing acceptance of Nicaea.
Revived in the 20th century in Oneness Pentecostalism.

positions.name: Pre-Nicene Logos theology
positions.oneLine: The one God has from eternity his Word (Logos) and Wisdom, who comes forth as a distinct person to create, reveal and save — truly divine, but described as second in order.
coreClaims: The Father is the ultimate source (arche) of deity.
The Word is God's own reason, ‘begotten’ or ‘put forth’ for creation and revelation; the Spirit likewise.
Father, Son and Spirit are distinct in number but share one substance or power (Tertullian).
The Son mediates between the transcendent Father and the world; Old Testament theophanies are appearances of the Son.
positions.origin: Developed by second-century Apologists (Justin Martyr, Athenagoras, Theophilus of Antioch, who first used trias c. 180), Irenaeus, Hippolytus, Tertullian and Origen, drawing on John's prologue, Jewish Wisdom literature and Middle Platonism.
strongestArguments: It allowed Christians to speak of Jesus as truly divine and personally distinct while keeping one source of deity.
It used the Bible's own Word and Wisdom categories and could explain to educated pagans how God relates to the world.
Tertullian's and Origen's vocabulary (substantia, persona, hypostasis, eternal generation) became the building blocks of later orthodoxy.
strongestObjections: Its ranking language (‘second God’, ‘in the second place’) left the Son's full equality unclear and fed Arianism.
Some versions had the Word become a distinct person only for creation (‘two-stage’ Logos), implying the Son is not eternally Son.
Its Platonic mediator concept assumed the high God cannot touch the world directly — a premise Nicenes later rejected.
responses: Defenders note that ranking expressed order of origin, not inferiority of nature — the reading Nicenes later made explicit.
Origen already taught that there was no time when the Son was not, anticipating Nicaea.
consequences: Provided both the vocabulary of Nicene orthodoxy and the premises of Arianism.
Shaped Christian apologetics in the Greco-Roman world.

positions.name: Arianism (and Homoian / Heteroousian successors)
positions.oneLine: The Son is the first and highest of God's works, created or begotten before time, through whom all else was made — divine by grace, not by nature equal to the unbegotten Father.
coreClaims: God alone is unbegotten, without beginning, unchangeable; the Son, being begotten, has a beginning: ‘there was when he was not’.
The Son was made ‘out of nothing’ by the Father's will, before all ages, and is the agent of creation.
The Son is ‘God’ in a derivative sense and worthy of honour, but is not of the Father's essence.

(Homoians, 359) The Son is ‘like the Father according to the Scriptures’; non-biblical terms like ousia should be banned. (Anomoeans) The Son is unlike the Father in essence, since ‘unbegotten’ defines God's essence.
The Spirit is a creature of the Son.
positions.origin: Arius, presbyter of Baucalis in Alexandria, clashed with Bishop Alexander c. 318; he drew support from Eusebius of Nicomedia and others trained in the school of Lucian of Antioch. After Nicaea the movement fragmented into Homoians (Acacius, Ulfilas, Valens), Anomoeans (Aetius, Eunomius) and others.
strongestArguments: It takes literally the biblical language of the Son's subordination, obedience, ignorance of the hour and prayer to the Father.
It protects the absolute uniqueness and impassibility of the unbegotten God, as the philosophical theology of the day demanded.
‘Begotten’ naturally implies a beginning; a Son as old as his Father seemed incoherent.
Homoians argued that keeping to scriptural language avoided importing pagan metaphysics (ousia) into the creed.
strongestObjections: Athanasius: Christians worship the Son and are baptised into his name; worshipping a creature is idolatry.
Only God can unite creatures to God; a created mediator cannot deify or save (On the Incarnation 54).
If the Father was once not Father, God changes — undermining the very immutability Arians wanted to protect.
John 1:1–3 says all things were made through the Word; if the Son was made, he made himself.
Proverbs 8:22 refers in context to Wisdom and, Athanasius argued, to the incarnate humanity.
responses: Arians replied that worship of the Son is relative honour, given at the Father's command (Philippians 2:9–11; Hebrews 1:6).
Eunomius argued that clear thinking requires that ‘unbegotten’ names God's essence, so the begotten must differ in essence.
Homoians argued that the Nicene term was unbiblical and Sabellian, and won majorities at councils in 359–360.
consequences: Sixty years of exiles, rival bishops and imperial interventions (325–381).

Through Ulfilas, Homoian Christianity became the faith of the Goths, Vandals, Burgundians and Lombards; the Vandal persecution of Nicene Christians in North Africa (5th c.) and the conversion of Visigothic Spain (589) followed.

‘Arian’ remained a byword in later polemics; Isaac Newton, William Whiston and Samuel Clarke revived Arian-like views in the 18th century, and Jehovah's Witnesses today hold a Christology similar in structure (the Son as first creation).

positions.name: Homoiousian theology (‘Semi-Arianism’)
positions.oneLine: The Son is ‘like in essence’ (homoiousios) to the Father — truly God's Son by nature, yet distinct enough to avoid Sabellian confusion.
coreClaims: The Son is a true Son, sharing the Father's kind of being, not a creature made from nothing.
‘Same essence’ (homoousios) risks merging Father and Son into one person (Sabellianism) or implying a material substance divided between them.
‘Like in essence’ preserves both real sonship and real distinction.
Many held a cautious view of the Spirit (some became Pneumatomachians).
positions.origin: A large conservative Eastern party, articulated by Basil of Ancyra and George of Laodicea at the Synod of Ancyra (358), reacting against the radical Anomoeans.
strongestArguments: It firmly rejected Arius' creaturely Son while answering real fears that homoousios was modalist (the word had been rejected at Antioch in 268).
Its formula seemed closer to biblical images (image, radiance) of the Son's likeness to the Father.
It represented the actual majority of Eastern bishops in the 350s.
strongestObjections: Athanasius argued that ‘likeness’ applies to qualities, not essences; if the Son is only like God, he is not God.
The formula could not exclude Homoians, who also said ‘like’, and so failed to stop Arian drift.
Two essences that are merely similar imply two gods.
responses: Athanasius (De Synodis, 359) recognised the Homoiousians as ‘brothers’ who meant what Nicaea meant, opening reconciliation.
The Cappadocians, partly from this milieu, showed that homoousios could be read without Sabellianism by distinguishing ousia and hypostasis.
consequences: Its alliance with Athanasius and the Cappadocians created the coalition that triumphed at Constantinople (381).
The pejorative label ‘Semi-Arian’ (from Epiphanius) obscured for centuries how anti-Arian this party was.

positions.name: Pneumatomachianism (Macedonianism)
positions.oneLine: The Son is of the Father's essence (or like it), but the Holy Spirit is a ministering power or the highest of creatures, not God.
coreClaims: Scripture never explicitly calls the Spirit ‘God’ or commands prayer to the Spirit.
The Spirit is a servant sent by Father and Son, of a rank between God and creatures.
Glory should be given to the Father through the Son in the Spirit, not ‘with’ the Spirit.
positions.origin: Emerged c. 360 in Egypt (the Tropici, answered in Athanasius' Letters to Serapion) and in Asia Minor around Eustathius of Sebaste; named after Macedonius of Constantinople.
strongestArguments: The New Testament's explicit language about the Spirit's deity is sparse compared with that about the Son.
The Spirit is consistently ‘sent’ and ‘given’, suggesting a subordinate role.
Cautious biblicism: they would not confess more than Scripture plainly said.
strongestObjections: The Spirit is included in the one baptismal name (Matthew 28:19) and lying to the Spirit is lying to God (Acts 5:3–4).
The Spirit sanctifies and deifies; only God can make holy (Athanasius, Letters to Serapion; Basil, On the Holy Spirit).
If the Spirit were a creature, baptism would be into a creature.
responses: Pneumatomachians replied that inclusion in a formula shows association, not identity of nature.
Gregory of Nazianzus answered that revelation is progressive: the Spirit's deity is ‘suggested’ in the New Testament and clarified by the Spirit's own presence in the Church.
consequences: Produced Basil's On the Holy Spirit and Gregory's Fifth Theological Oration.
Condemned at Constantinople (381), whose creed expanded the article on the Spirit.

positions.name: Nicene orthodoxy (homoousios)
positions.oneLine: The Son is ‘God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God, begotten not made, of one essence (homoousios) with the Father’; the Spirit is worshipped and glorified with them.
coreClaims: The Son is eternally begotten of the Father's own essence, not created; there was never a time when the Father was without the Son.
Father and Son are homoousios — the same in deity, distinct in that one begets and the other is begotten.
The Holy Spirit is Lord and Giver of life, proceeding from the Father, worshipped and glorified together with Father and Son (381).
The incarnation of the true God is necessary for salvation: only God can restore the image of God and give incorruption.
positions.origin: Defined at the Council of Nicaea (325) against Arius, championed by Alexander and Athanasius of Alexandria, Marcellus of Ancyra and Western bishops (Hilary of Poitiers, Ossius of Córdoba), and reaffirmed with the Spirit article at Constantinople (381).
strongestArguments: It alone fits the New Testament's worship of Jesus and the application to him of YHWH texts (e.g. Philippians 2:10–11 / Isaiah 45:23; John 12:41 / Isaiah 6).
Soteriological argument: only true God incarnate can unite humanity to God (‘He was made man that we might be made God’).
It preserves real distinction (against modalism) and real unity (against Arian ditheism or polytheism).
It has been the shared confession of nearly all churches for 1,600 years, across Greek, Latin, Syriac, Coptic, Armenian, Ge'ez and modern languages.
strongestObjections: The key term homoousios is not in Scripture and had been rejected at Antioch (268); critics call it the Hellenisation of the gospel (Harnack).
It was enforced by imperial power, which raises questions about whether it was truly the church's free consensus.
Unitarians and others argue that ‘three persons, one God’ is logically incoherent or unintelligible.
Texts of the Son's subordination and ignorance (Mark 13:32; John 14:28; 1 Corinthians 15:28) seem to be explained away.
responses: Nicenes reply that a non-biblical word was needed precisely because Arians could agree to every biblical phrase while meaning something else.
Imperial power backed Arians and Homoians as often as Nicenes (under Constantius II and Valens); Nicaea prevailed through argument and broad reception, not only force.
The doctrine claims to be a grammar safeguarding mystery, not a mathematical claim; ‘one’ and ‘three’ refer to different things (essence, hypostasis).
Subordination texts are read of the incarnate Son's humanity or of the Son's eternal origin (order, not inferiority).
consequences: Produced the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed, recited in the liturgy of most churches worldwide.
Established the model of ecumenical councils as means of settling doctrine — and of imperial involvement in doctrine.
Became the boundary marker distinguishing historic Christian bodies from nontrinitarian movements.

positions.name: Cappadocian formulation: one ousia, three hypostases
positions.oneLine: God is one in essence (ousia) and three in hypostases, each person distinguished only by an incommunicable property: the Father unbegotten, the Son begotten, the Spirit proceeding.
coreClaims: Ousia (essence) names what is common; hypostasis names what is particular — as the general to the particular.
The Father is the ‘cause’ and source (monarchia) of Son and Spirit, but they are co-eternal and equal.
All divine actions toward the world are one action, from the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit — so there are not three gods.
The divine essence is incomprehensible; we know God through his energies and works, never by grasping his essence (against Eunomius).
The Spirit is homotimos (of equal honour) with Father and Son.
positions.origin: Worked out c. 360–390 by Basil of Caesarea, his brother Gregory of Nyssa, their friend Gregory of Nazianzus, with their sister Macrina an influence on Nyssa; drawing on Athanasius and the Homoiousians, against the Anomoean Eunomius and the Pneumatomachians.
strongestArguments: It resolved the terminological confusion of the 4th century, reconciling Nicenes and Homoiousians.
It safeguards both the Father's monarchy (one source) and the full equality of the persons.
Its apophatic emphasis (God's essence is unknowable) fits biblical reticence and answers Eunomius' rationalism.
The unity of divine action (Gregory of Nyssa, To Ablabius) explains why three persons are not three gods.
strongestObjections: The ‘general/particular’ analogy (as humanity to Peter, James and John) seems to make the persons three instances of a genus — tritheism (as John Philoponus later concluded).
Western critics (and later Filioque defenders) argue that grounding unity in the Father's monarchy risks subordinating the Son and Spirit.
Some modern scholars argue the Cappadocians were less ‘social’ than 20th-century readers claim, so appeals to them are anachronistic.
responses: Gregory of Nyssa explicitly denies that the analogy implies three gods, since divine nature is not divided or numbered like human nature and the persons' action is one.
The Father's monarchy is a monarchy of origin, not of rank; the Son and Spirit possess all that the Father has except being unbegotten.
consequences: Became the classical formulation of Eastern Orthodox Trinitarian theology and was received by the Council of Constantinople (381).
Its terms entered Latin as una essentia, tres personae (with lasting translation difficulties between hypostasis and persona).
Its distinction between essence and energies was developed by Gregory Palamas (14th c.).

positions.name: Filioque: double procession (Western)
positions.oneLine: The Holy Spirit proceeds eternally from the Father and the Son as from one principle — so the creed may say ‘who proceeds from the Father and the Son’.
coreClaims: The Spirit is the Spirit of the Son as well as of the Father (Galatians 4:6; Romans 8:9); the Son sends and breathes the Spirit (John 15:26; 20:22).
Divine persons are distinguished by relations of origin; unless the Spirit proceeds from the Son, Son and Spirit would not be distinguished from each other (Anselm, Aquinas).
The Father is principally the source; the Son receives from the Father the capacity to breathe the Spirit (Augustine: principaliter from the Father).
The Spirit is the mutual love and gift of Father and Son.
positions.origin: Taught by Latin fathers (Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine); inserted into the creed in Spain at Toledo III (589) against Arian subordination of the Son; spread in Frankish lands under Charlemagne; adopted in Rome's liturgy c. 1014; defined at Lyon II (1274) and Florence (1439).
strongestArguments: It expresses the full equality of Father and Son: all that the Father has belongs to the Son (John 16:15), except being Father.
Scripture calls the Spirit ‘the Spirit of his Son’ and depicts the Son sending the Spirit.
Some Greek Fathers (Cyril of Alexandria, Maximus the Confessor) spoke of the Spirit proceeding ‘through the Son’, which Latins see as compatible.
Historically it guarded against Arianism in Visigothic Spain.
strongestObjections: The original creed of 381 said ‘from the Father’; a single regional church may not alter an ecumenical creed (Council of Ephesus canon 7 forbids a different creed).
Two sources of the Spirit compromise the Father's monarchy, or else merge Father and Son into one impersonal principle (Photius).
It subordinates the Spirit to the Son, encouraging ‘Christomonism’ and an institutional, Spirit-neglecting ecclesiology (modern Orthodox critics such as Vladimir Lossky).
Pope Leo III himself (c. 810) had the original creed engraved on silver shields in St Peter's, refusing the insertion.
responses: Latins argue the addition clarifies rather than changes the faith, and was made for pastoral need against Arians.

The 1995 Vatican clarification states that the Father is the sole ‘source without source’ and that the Latin procedit (from the Father and the Son) is not the same as the Greek ekporeuesthai (from the Father alone as origin).
Rome itself uses the creed without the Filioque in Greek and with Eastern Catholics; several Anglican provinces have proposed or adopted its omission.
consequences: A major doctrinal grievance behind the East–West estrangement and the 1054 schism.
Central agenda item at the reunion councils of Lyon (1274) and Florence (1439).
Ongoing ecumenical dialogue: the 2003 North American Orthodox–Catholic statement concluded it need no longer be church-dividing if handled well.

positions.name: Monopatrism: procession from the Father alone (Eastern)
positions.oneLine: The Father alone is the eternal source and cause of the Son (by begetting) and of the Spirit (by procession); the Son's role in the Spirit's sending belongs to the economy or, at most, to an eternal manifestation ‘through the Son’.
coreClaims: Each hypostatic property belongs to one person only: being unbegotten and causing belongs to the Father alone.
John 15:26 says the Spirit ‘proceeds from the Father’; the Son ‘sends’ the Spirit in time (the economy).
The Creed of 381, confirmed by later ecumenical councils, may not be changed except by an ecumenical council.
The Spirit eternally shines forth or rests on the Son (Gregory of Cyprus, 13th c.), but takes origin from the Father alone.
positions.origin: Implicit in the Cappadocians' monarchy of the Father; formulated against the Latin Filioque by Patriarch Photius of Constantinople in his encyclical (867) and Mystagogy of the Holy Spirit; refined by Gregory of Cyprus and Gregory Palamas.
strongestArguments: It keeps the exact words of Christ in John 15:26 and of the ecumenical creed.
It preserves the Father's monarchy, the Cappadocian guarantee of divine unity.
John of Damascus already wrote that the Spirit is ‘from the Father’ and ‘of the Son’, but ‘we do not say from the Son’ (Exact Exposition 1.8).
Ecclesially it guards conciliarity against a single see altering the common faith.
strongestObjections: Latin theologians argue that without a relation of origin between Son and Spirit their distinction is undefined.
Scripture's ‘Spirit of the Son’ language suggests an eternal, not merely temporal, relation.
Some Greek Fathers (Cyril, Maximus) used ‘through the Son’ language that seems to give the Son an eternal role.
responses: Orthodox theologians answer that persons are distinguished by their unique mode of origin from the Father (begetting vs procession), which suffices.
Gregory of Cyprus and Palamas distinguish eternal procession (from the Father alone) from an eternal manifestation or radiance through the Son — accepting ‘through the Son’ in that sense.
Maximus the Confessor's Letter to Marinus defended the Western usage only as meaning the Son is not the cause.
consequences: Defines the Orthodox side of a millennium-long dispute, rehearsed at Lyon (1274) and Florence (1439).
Shapes Orthodox pneumatology and ecclesiology (emphasis on the Spirit's freedom and the conciliar church).
Agreed statements since the 1990s have narrowed but not closed the gap.

positions.name: Classical (Latin/Scholastic) Trinitarianism
positions.oneLine: One utterly simple God subsists as three persons who are nothing other than subsisting relations of origin — paternity, filiation and spiration — known to us only through revelation.
coreClaims: The divine essence is one and numerically identical in all three persons; the persons are not parts or instances of a kind.
The persons are distinguished only by opposed relations of origin (Father–Son; Father and Son–Spirit).
All works of the Trinity toward creation are undivided (opera ad extra indivisa sunt), though appropriated to particular persons.
Analogies (memory–understanding–will; lover–beloved–love) are aids to contemplation, not proofs.
The Trinity is a revealed mystery beyond natural reason.
positions.origin: Rooted in Augustine's De Trinitate (c. 400–420) and the Athanasian Creed (Quicunque vult, c. 500), systematised by Anselm, Peter Lombard and Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae I, qq. 27–43), confirmed at Lateran IV (1215) against Joachim of Fiore, and received by Reformation confessions.
proponentsOther: contemporary: Gilles Emery, Matthew Levering, Fred Sanders (broadly)
strongestArguments: It guards divine unity rigorously, avoiding any hint of three gods.
It offers a coherent account of how persons are distinguished (relations) without dividing the essence.
It has shaped Western liturgy, mysticism and theology for 1,500 years and has deep patristic roots in both East and West.
Its doctrine of inseparable operations explains biblical texts in which Father, Son and Spirit all create, raise and indwell.
strongestObjections: Eastern critics argue that it begins with the one essence and struggles to reach real persons, tending toward modalism.
Social Trinitarians say ‘subsisting relations’ are too abstract to be persons who love and speak to one another, as the Gospels depict.
Rahner complained that it made the Trinity irrelevant to piety: most Christians would be ‘mere monotheists’ in practice.
Analytic philosophers question whether ‘simple’ and ‘three really distinct persons’ are logically consistent.
responses: Defenders argue the ‘Western starts with essence, East with persons’ contrast (de Régnon paradigm) is a 19th-century oversimplification.
Augustine and Aquinas insist the persons are really distinct and mutually indwelling; relations are not less but more personal than ‘individuals’.
Classical theologians answer that modern ‘persons’ (centres of consciousness) is a different concept from patristic hypostasis, and importing it produces tritheism.
consequences: Foundation of Western dogmatic theology, catechisms and the Athanasian Creed's place in Western liturgy.
Supported the theological rationale for the Filioque.
A reference point in contemporary debates with social Trinitarians and analytic philosophers.

positions.name: Classical theism and divine simplicity
positions.oneLine: God is pure act — without parts, composition, change or passive potency — so that God's essence, existence and attributes are identical; he is eternal, immutable and impassible.
coreClaims: God is not composed of parts, matter and form, essence and existence, or substance and accidents (Aquinas, ST I q. 3).
God's attributes (goodness, wisdom, power) are identical with his essence, distinguished only in our understanding.
God is immutable and impassible: he is not acted upon by creatures, though he acts in love toward them.
God is timelessly eternal and knows all things, including the future, in one eternal act.
Creatures depend wholly on God; God does not depend on creatures.
positions.origin: Assumed by the Fathers (Irenaeus, Athanasius, Augustine), formalised by Boethius, Anselm, Maimonides and Aquinas, defined at Lateran IV (1215) and Vatican I (1870), and confessed in Reformed and Lutheran confessions (Westminster Confession 2.1: God is ‘without body, parts, or passions’).
proponentsOther: contemporary: Brian Davies, Edward Feser, James Dolezal, Katherin Rogers
strongestArguments: If God had parts, something would be prior to God (the parts) or would compose him; God would not be the first cause.
It secures God's absolute sovereignty, reliability (he cannot change his promises) and aseity.
Eastern and Western Fathers, medieval Jewish and Islamic philosophers, and the confessions all shared it — a broad consensus.
It protects divine love from being needy or self-interested: God loves freely, not to gain anything.
strongestObjections: Alvin Plantinga (1980) argued that if God is identical with his properties, God is a property — absurd.
It seems to conflict with biblical depictions of God relenting, grieving and responding (Genesis 6:6; Exodus 32:14; Jonah 3:10).
If God's knowledge of the world is identical to his essence, and the world could have been otherwise, God's essence seems contingent (modal collapse objection).
Eastern Orthodox theologians accept simplicity but reject a strict identity of essence and energies (Palamas).
responses: Classical theists say biblical language of emotion and change is analogical, describing God's relation to changing creatures.
Thomists answer the modal-collapse objection by locating contingency in creatures' relation to God, not in God.
They argue that Plantinga's critique assumes a modern, Platonist view of properties foreign to the classical tradition.
consequences: Defines the boundary in contemporary debates with open theism, process theology and some social Trinitarianism.
Shaped Christian, Jewish and Islamic philosophical theology together.
Since c. 2010 a renewed ‘retrieval of classical theism’ among Reformed, Baptist and Catholic writers.

positions.name: Social Trinitarianism
positions.oneLine: God is three distinct persons — each a centre of knowing, willing and loving — whose unity is a perfect communion of mutual indwelling (perichoresis), a model for human community.
coreClaims: Father, Son and Spirit are persons in a full sense, with real I–Thou relationships, as the Gospels portray.
The divine unity is a unity of love and mutual indwelling rather than an undifferentiated essence.
Personhood and relationship are ontologically primary: ‘being as communion’ (Zizioulas).
The Trinity offers a pattern for church, society and politics — equality without uniformity, against hierarchy and individualism (Moltmann, Boff).
positions.origin: Antecedents in Richard of St Victor (12th c.) and readings of the Cappadocians; developed in the 20th century by Jürgen Moltmann (The Trinity and the Kingdom, 1980), John Zizioulas (Being as Communion, 1985), Leonardo Boff (Trinity and Society, 1986) and analytic philosophers (Cornelius Plantinga Jr., Richard Swinburne, William Hasker).
strongestArguments: It takes seriously the Gospels' depiction of the Son praying to and loving the Father.
It makes the Trinity practically meaningful for spirituality, ethics and ecclesiology (Rahner's complaint answered).
It explains how God can be love eternally (1 John 4:8): love needs a lover and a beloved.
It resonated strongly in Latin American liberation theology and in African communal anthropology (ubuntu).
strongestObjections: Tritheism: three centres of consciousness and will contradict the Nicene and Chalcedonian teaching of one divine will (Constantinople III, 681).
It anachronistically reads modern ideas of ‘person’ into patristic hypostasis.
Projection: social models often find in God the politics the theologian already favours (Karen Kilby, ‘projection’ critique, 2000).
Historians (Ayres, Holmes) argue the Cappadocians held a strongly classical view of unity, undermining the claimed patristic precedent.
responses: Social Trinitarians reply that perichoresis — mutual indwelling — secures unity without collapsing persons.
Some revise the model to avoid three wills, emphasising relational ontology rather than three minds.
They argue that analogy runs both ways: the church is meant to image God (John 17:21), so ethical application is biblical, not projection.
consequences: Widely influential in late-20th-century ecclesiology, ecumenism, feminist and liberation theology.
Provoked a vigorous classical-theism counter-movement and debates (e.g. evangelical ‘eternal functional subordination’ controversy, 2016).
Shaped popular evangelical language of God as ‘relationship’ or ‘divine dance’.

positions.name: Oneness Pentecostalism (outside historic Nicene orthodoxy)
positions.oneLine: God is absolutely one person who has revealed himself as Father in creation, as Son in the incarnation, and as Holy Spirit in regeneration — and the one name of God is Jesus.
coreClaims: God is one, indivisible person, not three persons; ‘Father’, ‘Son’ and ‘Holy Spirit’ are titles or manifestations.
Jesus is the fullness of the Godhead bodily (Colossians 2:9): the Father dwelling in the human Son.
The ‘Son’ refers to the incarnate humanity; there was no eternal Son distinct from the Father.
Baptism should be performed ‘in the name of Jesus Christ’ (Acts 2:38), which fulfils Matthew 28:19's ‘name’ (singular).
Many (e.g. UPCI) teach that repentance, Jesus' Name baptism and Spirit baptism with tongues together constitute the new birth (Acts 2:38).
positions.origin: At the Arroyo Seco world-wide camp meeting near Los Angeles (1913), R. E. McAlister observed that the apostles baptised only in Jesus' name; Frank Ewart, Glenn Cook and G. T. Haywood developed a Oneness doctrine of God (1914). When the Assemblies of God adopted a Trinitarian Statement of Fundamental Truths (1916), about a quarter of its ministers left; the Pentecostal Assemblies of the World and later the United Pentecostal Church International (1945) were formed.
proponentsOther: T. D. Jakes (raised Oneness; affirmed a modalistic-leaning view, later nuanced)
strongestArguments: It defends uncompromising biblical monotheism using only biblical vocabulary, without ‘person’, ‘essence’ or ‘Trinity’.
Every recorded baptism in Acts uses the name of Jesus (Acts 2:38; 8:16; 10:48; 19:5).
It affirms Jesus' full deity emphatically: Jesus is not one-third of God but ‘the mighty God, the everlasting Father’ (Isaiah 9:6).
It claims continuity with early monarchian believers whom Tertullian admitted were ‘the majority’ of simple believers (Against Praxeas 3).
strongestObjections: The Gospels show the Son and Father in mutual, eternal relationship: the Son was with the Father ‘before the world was’ (John 17:5, 24) and was sent from heaven.
It repeats the ancient modalism condemned by the early church; ‘Father’ and ‘Son’ become roles rather than real relations.
Critics argue the Acts formula is a description (‘on Jesus' authority’), not a liturgical formula replacing Matthew 28:19; the Didache (c. 100) already uses the triadic formula.
Trinitarian Pentecostals regard its requirement of Jesus' Name baptism and tongues for salvation as adding to the gospel.
responses: Oneness theologians distinguish their view from Sabellianism: God's manifestations are simultaneous, not successive, and the Son's prayers are the humanity's communion with the indwelling deity.
They argue that John 17:5 speaks of the glory planned for the Son in God's foreknowledge.
They contend that post-biblical councils, not Scripture, introduced three persons.
consequences: A major split in early Pentecostalism (1916), still dividing Pentecostal fellowships.

Strong growth worldwide: the UPCI, Pentecostal Assemblies of the World, Apostolic churches in Mexico and Colombia (Iglesia Pentecostal Unida de Colombia), the True Jesus Church in China and Taiwan (founded 1917, with Oneness and Sabbatarian views), and many African Apostolic churches; global adherents often estimated at 20–30 million or more.
Recurrent tension and dialogue with Trinitarian Pentecostals (e.g. 2007 Oneness–Trinitarian Pentecostal dialogue).

positions.name: Unitarianism and Socinianism (outside historic Nicene orthodoxy)
positions.oneLine: God is one person, the Father; Jesus is the Messiah — a human being uniquely chosen, empowered and exalted by God — and the Holy Spirit is God's power, not a person.
coreClaims: Scripture's ‘one God’ is the Father alone (1 Corinthians 8:6; John 17:3; 1 Timothy 2:5).
Jesus is a true man, virgin-born (in Socinian form) or born naturally (in later liberal forms), raised and given authority by God.
The doctrine of the Trinity is a post-biblical corruption arising from Greek philosophy and imperial politics.
Reason and conscience must judge doctrine; doctrines that are unintelligible cannot be required for salvation.
(Socinian) Christ's death is an example and a confirmation of God's promises, not a penal satisfaction.
positions.origin: Radical Reformation: Michael Servetus (On the Errors of the Trinity, 1531; burned at Geneva 1553); Laelius and Faustus Socinus; the Polish Brethren and the Racovian Catechism (1605); Francis Dávid and the Unitarian Church of Transylvania, protected by the Edict of Torda (1568); in England, John Biddle and Theophilus Lindsey (Essex Street Chapel, 1774); in New England, William Ellery Channing's Baltimore sermon (1819) and the American Unitarian Association (1825).
strongestArguments: The Shema and Jesus' own reaffirmation of it (Mark 12:29) speak of one God who is clearly the Father.
Many New Testament texts distinguish God from Jesus (‘the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ’).
The technical terms of the creeds are absent from Scripture and arose amid philosophical and political struggles.
It stresses moral religion, freedom of conscience and toleration — the Transylvanian Unitarians were early advocates of religious liberty.
strongestObjections: The New Testament applies divine names, worship and creative agency to Jesus (John 1:1–3; 20:28; Hebrews 1:8–10; Philippians 2:10–11).
A merely human saviour cannot unite humanity to God or bear divine judgement (Athanasius, Anselm).
Historically, many Unitarian bodies moved from biblical unitarianism to non-creedal liberal religion, which critics see as the logic of rejecting Christ's deity.
It requires reading the earliest Christian worship of Jesus as a deviation from apostolic faith rather than its expression.
responses: Unitarians answer that worship of Jesus is honour delegated by God, and ‘God’ applied to Jesus is representative (as with Moses in Exodus 7:1 or judges in Psalm 82).
They argue that Christianity's credibility in an age of reason requires freeing it from incomprehensible dogma.
Biblical Unitarians today distinguish themselves from the post-Christian Unitarian Universalist movement.
consequences: Servetus' execution (1553) became a landmark in debates on religious toleration (Castellio, Concerning Heretics, 1554).
The Unitarian Church of Transylvania survives today, mainly among ethnic Hungarians in Romania.
American Unitarianism shaped New England intellectual culture (Harvard Divinity School), Transcendentalism and, after merger with Universalists (1961), the Unitarian Universalist Association.
Anti-Trinitarian laws in Britain (repealed by the Doctrine of the Trinity Act 1813).

positions.name: Latter-day Saint Godhead (outside historic Nicene orthodoxy)
positions.oneLine: The Father, the Son and the Holy Ghost are three distinct beings, one in purpose; the Father and the Son have glorified bodies of flesh and bone.
coreClaims: Father, Son and Holy Ghost are three separate personages united in will, purpose and love.
God the Father is an exalted, embodied being; the Holy Ghost is a personage of spirit.
The Nicene doctrine of one substance is part of a ‘Great Apostasy’ corrected by restoration through Joseph Smith.
Humans are spirit children of heavenly parents with potential for exaltation.
positions.origin: Joseph Smith's First Vision (accounts from 1832–1842) and later teachings, especially the King Follett discourse (1844) and Doctrine and Covenants 130 (1843).
strongestArguments: At Jesus' baptism and in Stephen's vision the Father and Son appear as distinct beings.
Jesus' prayer that his disciples be ‘one, as we are one’ (John 17:21) suggests unity of purpose, not of substance.
Latter-day Saints present it as a restoration of biblical, pre-Hellenistic belief, confirmed by modern revelation.
strongestObjections: Historic Christian bodies regard three distinct gods as incompatible with biblical monotheism (Isaiah 43:10; 44:6).
Divine embodiment contradicts John 4:24 (‘God is a Spirit’) and the classical doctrine of God's infinity.
The restoration claim depends on modern revelation that other Christians do not accept.
responses: LDS writers argue that ‘one God’ in Scripture refers to a united Godhead, and that early Jewish and Christian thought was more anthropomorphic than later creeds.
consequences: A key reason most Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant bodies do not recognise LDS baptism (e.g. Catholic Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, 2001).
Underlies ongoing interfaith dialogue between LDS and evangelical scholars since the 1990s.

positions.name: Open theism
positions.oneLine: God is a loving, relational being who genuinely responds to creatures; because creatures are truly free, the future is partly open and God knows it as possibilities, not settled facts.
coreClaims: Love is God's chief attribute; God seeks real, reciprocal relationship with free creatures.
Libertarian free will means future free choices do not yet exist to be known; God knows all that is knowable.
God can change his mind, be grieved, take risks and be surprised, as Scripture says (Genesis 6:6; Jeremiah 3:7; Jonah 3:10).
God remains omnipotent and sovereign and will certainly achieve his ultimate purposes.
Classical immutability and impassibility owe more to Greek philosophy than to the Bible.
positions.origin: Antecedents in Calcidius and some 19th-century Methodists (Lorenzo McCabe); crystallised in evangelical theology with Richard Rice (The Openness of God, 1980) and the multi-author The Openness of God (1994); debated sharply in the Evangelical Theological Society (2001–2003), which declined to expel Clark Pinnock and John Sanders.
proponentsOther: Thomas Jay Oord (open and relational, nearer process)
strongestArguments: It reads straightforwardly the many biblical passages in which God repents, tests, asks questions and changes course.
It offers a strong theodicy: God is not the author of evil, because he did not eternally ordain particular evils.
It makes petitionary prayer genuinely effective.
It aims to free Christian theology from Hellenistic assumptions while staying evangelical on Scripture and creation.
strongestObjections: Biblical prophecies of free human acts (Peter's denial, Judas, Cyrus named in Isaiah 44:28) seem to require exhaustive foreknowledge.
Isaiah 46:9–10 presents God's knowledge of ‘the end from the beginning’ as proof of his deity.
Classical theists argue that a God who learns and risks cannot guarantee his promises or the final victory of good.
It treats anthropomorphic texts literally but not others (God's ‘arm’, ‘eyes’), applying an inconsistent hermeneutic.
responses: Open theists answer that God can predict or bring about specific events without foreknowing every free act.
They distinguish God's immutable character from his mutable experience and plans.
They argue that the classical reading equally selects some texts (Malachi 3:6) as controlling over others.
consequences: Divided North American evangelical institutions in the 1990s–2000s (ETS debates; the Baptist General Conference controversy over Gregory Boyd).
Fuelled renewed defence of classical theism and of Arminian ‘simple foreknowledge’ and Molinist alternatives.
Connected with ‘relational theology’ movements in Wesleyan and Pentecostal circles.

positions.name: Process theology
positions.oneLine: Reality is a creative process of events, and God is its supreme instance: dipolar (with an eternal ‘primordial’ and an ever-growing ‘consequent’ nature), luring the world by persuasive love rather than coercive power.
coreClaims: Becoming, not static being, is fundamental; God too is in process.
God has a primordial nature (eternal possibilities) and a consequent nature (God's experience of the world, which grows).
God acts by persuasion, offering each moment its best possibility (the ‘initial aim’), never by unilateral coercion.
God is genuinely affected by the world's joys and sufferings — ‘the fellow-sufferer who understands’ (Whitehead).
God includes the world without being identical to it (panentheism); creation ex nihilo is usually rejected.
positions.origin: From Alfred North Whitehead's metaphysics (Process and Reality, 1929) and Charles Hartshorne's neoclassical theism (Man's Vision of God, 1941); developed theologically by John B. Cobb Jr., Schubert Ogden, Norman Pittenger, Marjorie Suchocki and David Ray Griffin, centred on Claremont, California.
strongestArguments: It offers a direct answer to the problem of evil: God does not prevent evil because God does not exercise coercive omnipotence.
It integrates theology with evolutionary science and a dynamic view of nature.
It takes seriously the biblical God who suffers with his people and whose love is vulnerable.
It has been fruitful for ecological theology and for interreligious dialogue (especially with Buddhism).
strongestObjections: It abandons creation ex nihilo and God's omnipotence, which most Christians regard as essential.
It offers no assurance that good will finally triumph or of bodily resurrection.
Its God is ‘the great companion’ but arguably not the Lord worthy of worship.
Its Trinitarian theology is thin or reinterpretive; many process thinkers do not affirm a Nicene Trinity.
responses: Process theologians answer that persuasive love is a higher form of power than coercion, and that omnipotence as usually defined makes God responsible for evil.
They argue that objective immortality — every event preserved in God's memory — gives the world everlasting significance.
Some (e.g. Joseph Bracken) have developed process-Trinitarian models.
consequences: Influential in mainline Protestant seminaries in North America (1960s–1990s) and in ecological theology.
Provoked responses from classical theists and indirectly influenced open theism, which shares its relational emphasis while retaining creation ex nihilo.

controversies.title: The Arian Controversy: homoousios
controversies.question: Is the Son homoousios (of one essence) with the Father — or the first and greatest of God's creatures?
controversies.summary: From c. 318 to 381, the eastern Roman Empire argued over whether the Son of God is eternal and of the Father's own essence, or a creature made before time. Councils, emperors and exiles shaped the debate; the Nicene answer prevailed at Constantinople (381), while Homoian Christianity endured among the Germanic peoples for two more centuries.

sides.name: Nicene (homoousian)
sides.steelman: We worship Christ, we are baptised into his name, and we are saved by him. If he were a creature, our worship would be idolatry and our salvation a fiction — for no creature can join creatures to God. Scripture calls him the Word who was God, through whom all things were made: he cannot be one of the things made. ‘Of one essence’ is not a philosophical novelty; it is the only phrase our opponents could not twist to their meaning.
arguments: Christians already worshipped Jesus (Philippians 2:10–11; John 20:28; Pliny's letter of c. 112).
Only God can deify: ‘He was made man that we might be made God.’
If the Father was ever without the Son, God changed — and God is unchangeable.
All things were made through the Word (John 1:3); he therefore cannot be made.
counterArguments: Homoousios is unbiblical and was previously condemned at Antioch (268).
It confuses the persons (Sabellianism) or implies a material substance divided between Father and Son.

sides.name: Arian / Homoian
sides.steelman: We confess the Son as God's firstborn, the mighty agent of creation, worthy of honour beyond every creature. But God alone is unbegotten and without beginning. To say the Son shares the Father's very essence is either to make two unbegotten gods or to collapse the Son into the Father. Scripture says the Father is greater, that the Son learned obedience and did not know the hour. We keep to the words of Scripture; it is the Nicenes who have imported the language of the philosophers.
arguments: ‘Begotten’ implies a beginning; a Son co-eternal with his Father is incoherent.
The Son confesses the Father ‘greater’ and ‘the only true God’ (John 14:28; 17:3).
Proverbs 8:22 (LXX): Wisdom says ‘the Lord created me’.
Non-scriptural terms such as ousia should not be imposed as tests of faith (Homoian creed of 359–360).
counterArguments: Worship of a creature is idolatry.
Divine generation is not like human generation in time; the Father is eternally Father.

sides.name: Homoiousian (‘like in essence’)
sides.steelman: We reject Arius' creature-Son as firmly as anyone: the Son is truly from the Father, Son by nature. But ‘same essence’ sounds like Sabellius and Paul of Samosata. Say rather that he is ‘like in essence’ — truly the Father's image, never confused with him.
arguments: It avoids both Arian creaturehood and Sabellian confusion.
The Son is ‘the image of the invisible God’ — an image is like, not identical to, its original.
counterArguments: Likeness applies to qualities, not essences; something merely like God is not God.

timeline.text: Arius disputes with Bishop Alexander of Alexandria; he is excommunicated by an Egyptian synod (c. 321).
Council of Nicaea adopts homoousios; Arius exiled.
Athanasius exiled to Trier by the Council of Tyre — the first of five exiles.
Arius dies in Constantinople on the eve of his readmission.
‘Blasphemy of Sirmium’ forbids ousia language; radical Anomoeanism (Aetius, Eunomius) rises.
Councils of Ariminum and Seleucia impose the Homoian creed under Constantius II.
Council of Alexandria: Athanasius reconciles with those who mean the same by different terms.
Edict of Thessalonica (Theodosius I) makes Nicene faith the religion of the empire.
Council of Constantinople reaffirms Nicaea and confesses the Spirit's deity.
Visigothic Spain abandons Homoian Christianity at Toledo III.

resolution.text: Resolved for the imperial church at Constantinople (381) in favour of homoousios, after the Homoiousians were reconciled to Nicaea. Homoian (‘Arian’) churches persisted among Goths, Vandals and Lombards until the late 6th–7th centuries. Today nearly all churches confess the Nicene Creed; Jehovah's Witnesses and some Unitarians hold views structurally similar to Arius'.

consequences: The Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed became the shared creed of almost all Christians.
Established the pattern of ecumenical councils and imperial involvement in doctrine.
Created a religious divide between Nicene Romans and Homoian Germanic rulers in the post-Roman West.
Gave the Christian vocabulary of ousia and hypostasis, later needed for Christology.

controversies.title: The Filioque
controversies.question: Does the Holy Spirit proceed from the Father alone, or from the Father ‘and the Son’ (Filioque)?
controversies.summary: A single Latin word added to the Creed in Spain (589) became, after Photius (867), a central doctrinal point dividing Eastern and Western Christianity. The dispute combines Trinitarian theology (how the persons are distinguished) with ecclesiology (who may change an ecumenical creed).

sides.name: Western: ‘and the Son’
sides.steelman: Everything the Father has he gives to the Son, except being Father. The Spirit is called ‘the Spirit of his Son’, and the risen Christ breathes him on the apostles. If the Son had no part in the Spirit's eternal origin, nothing would distinguish Son from Spirit. We confess, with Augustine, that the Spirit proceeds principally from the Father, and from the Son as the Father's gift — one principle, not two. The phrase was added to defend the Son's equality against Arians, not to change the faith.
arguments: Galatians 4:6 and Romans 8:9: the Spirit belongs to the Son.
John 16:14–15: the Spirit receives from what is the Son's, and all that the Father has is the Son's.
Relations of origin are needed to distinguish the persons (Anselm, Aquinas).
Greek fathers (Cyril, Maximus) spoke of procession ‘through the Son’.
counterArguments: No regional church may alter the creed of an ecumenical council.
It undermines the Father's monarchy or blends Father and Son.

sides.name: Eastern: ‘from the Father’ (alone)
sides.steelman: Christ himself said the Spirit ‘proceeds from the Father’. The Fathers of 381 confessed exactly that, and the whole Church sealed it. The Father alone is the source of deity; the Son is begotten and the Spirit proceeds, each uniquely from him. To make the Son a second cause either divides the divine monarchy or turns Father and Son into a single impersonal principle. And when one bishop changes the creed of all, the conciliar nature of the Church itself is wounded.
arguments: John 15:26 says ‘from the Father’ without qualification.
Ephesus (431) forbade composing a different creed.
Personal properties are not shared: causing belongs to the Father alone.
The Son's sending of the Spirit is temporal (the economy), not eternal origin.
counterArguments: Eternal relations should be revealed by temporal missions.
Without a Son–Spirit relation of origin the persons are not clearly distinguished.

timeline.text: Creed of Constantinople: the Spirit ‘proceeds from the Father’.
Council of Ephesus forbids any other creed (canon 7).
Toledo III adds Filioque in Visigothic Spain.
Council of Aachen under Charlemagne endorses the Filioque; Pope Leo III affirms the doctrine but refuses to add it to the creed, displaying the original text on silver shields.
Photius' encyclical condemns the Filioque as heresy.
Filioque sung at Rome at the coronation of Emperor Henry II (traditional date).
Mutual excommunications; the Filioque among the charges.
Second Council of Lyon defines double procession; union short-lived.
Council of Florence: Laetentur Caeli union; rejected in the East.
Vatican clarification: the Father as sole source; Greek ekporeusis distinguished from Latin processio.
North American Orthodox–Catholic Consultation recommends the Catholic Church use the original creed.

resolution.text: Unresolved but softened. Catholics, Lutherans, Reformed and most Protestants retain the Filioque in liturgical use (Rome omits it in Greek); Eastern and Oriental Orthodox and the Assyrian Church of the East reject it. Agreed statements since 1995 suggest the theological gap is narrower than the historical polemic, while the ecclesiological question (authority to amend the creed) remains.

consequences: A lasting doctrinal marker of the East–West schism.
Shaped reunion councils (Lyon 1274, Florence 1439) and their failure.
Stimulated distinctive Orthodox pneumatology (Lossky) and Western reconsideration in the ecumenical age.

people.name: Theodotus of Byzantium (‘the Cobbler’)
people.summary: A learned leather-merchant from Byzantium who taught at Rome that Jesus was a man on whom the Spirit (Christ) descended at baptism; excommunicated by Bishop Victor of Rome c. 190. The founder of dynamic monarchianism.
keyIdeas: Jesus a mere man empowered at baptism

people.name: Noetus of Smyrna
people.summary: Teacher at Smyrna who taught that the Father himself was born, suffered and died — one God called Father or Son according to circumstance. Condemned by the presbyters of Smyrna; refuted in Hippolytus' Against Noetus.

people.name: Praxeas
people.summary: A confessor from Asia who brought modalist teaching to Rome and opposed the Montanists. Known only through Tertullian's Against Praxeas; some scholars think the name is a pseudonym for a known figure.

people.name: Eunomius of Cyzicus
people.summary: Leading Anomoean (Heteroousian) theologian, disciple of Aetius and briefly bishop of Cyzicus. He argued that ‘unbegotten’ defines God's essence, so the begotten Son is unlike the Father in essence, and that God's essence is knowable. Refuted by Basil and Gregory of Nyssa.
keyIdeas: The Son unlike the Father in essence

people.name: Ulfilas (Wulfila)
people.summary: ‘Apostle of the Goths’, consecrated bishop c. 341 by Eusebius of Nicomedia. He created the Gothic alphabet and translated the Bible into Gothic. A Homoian, he transmitted a non-Nicene Christianity to the Gothic peoples.

people.name: Basil of Ancyra
people.summary: Bishop of Ancyra and leader of the Homoiousian party; at the Synod of Ancyra (358) he argued that the Son is ‘like in essence’ to the Father, opposing both Arians and perceived Sabellians.

people.name: Michael Servetus
people.summary: Spanish physician and polymath who described pulmonary circulation and wrote On the Errors of the Trinity (1531) and The Restoration of Christianity (1553). Condemned by Catholic authorities, he escaped to Geneva, where he was tried and burned with Calvin's support in October 1553 — a key case in debates over toleration.
keyIdeas: Rejection of the Trinity of persons
Christ as the Son of the eternal God, not the eternal Son

people.name: Faustus Socinus (Fausto Sozzini)
people.summary: Italian theologian who settled in Poland (1579) and became the leading thinker of the Minor Reformed Church (Polish Brethren). Socinianism denied the Trinity, the pre-existence of Christ and penal satisfaction; its Racovian Catechism appeared in 1605.

people.name: Francis Dávid (Ferenc Dávid)
people.summary: Transylvanian reformer who moved from Catholicism through Lutheranism and Calvinism to Unitarianism, founding the Unitarian Church of Transylvania; court preacher to King John Sigismund, whose Edict of Torda (1568) granted religious freedom. He died in prison after opposing the invocation of Christ.

people.name: William Ellery Channing
people.summary: Boston Congregationalist minister whose 1819 Baltimore ordination sermon ‘Unitarian Christianity’ became the manifesto of American Unitarianism; an advocate of human dignity, moral religion and, later, abolition.

people.name: Frank J. Ewart
people.summary: Australian-born Pentecostal minister in Los Angeles who, after the 1913 Arroyo Seco camp meeting, formulated Oneness theology and in 1914 began rebaptising believers in Jesus' name. His The Phenomenon of Pentecost (1947) is an early movement history.

people.name: Clark Pinnock
people.summary: Canadian evangelical theologian who moved from Calvinism to Arminianism and then to open theism; lead author of The Openness of God (1994) and Most Moved Mover (2001).

people.name: Alfred North Whitehead
people.summary: English mathematician (co-author of Principia Mathematica) and Harvard philosopher whose process metaphysics (Process and Reality, 1929) became the basis of process theology.
keyIdeas: God as the lure of creative advance

people.name: Charles Hartshorne
people.summary: American philosopher who developed Whitehead's ideas into ‘neoclassical theism’ and panentheism, and revived the ontological argument in modal form.

people.name: John B. Cobb Jr.
people.summary: American Methodist theologian, born in Japan to missionary parents, the leading exponent of Christian process theology at Claremont; a pioneer of ecological theology and Buddhist–Christian dialogue.

people.name: John Zizioulas (Metropolitan of Pergamon)
people.summary: Greek Orthodox theologian and metropolitan whose Being as Communion (1985) argued that personhood and communion, grounded in the Father as cause, are ontologically primary — influential in ecumenical ecclesiology and social Trinitarianism.

works.title: Creed of Nicaea
works.author: Council of Nicaea
works.summary: The original creed of the Council of Nicaea, confessing the Son ‘begotten of the Father, the only-begotten, that is, of the essence of the Father… of one substance (homoousios) with the Father’, with anathemas against Arian phrases.
works.significance: The first creed issued by an ecumenical council and the foundation of all later Trinitarian orthodoxy.

works.title: Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed
works.author: Council of Constantinople
works.summary: The expanded creed associated with the Council of Constantinople (381), read at Chalcedon (451). It adds that the Spirit is ‘the Lord and Giver of life, who proceeds from the Father, who with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified’ and confesses ‘one holy catholic and apostolic Church’.
works.significance: The most widely shared creed in Christianity, recited in the liturgy of Orthodox, Oriental, Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran and many other churches (in the West with the Filioque).

works.title: Athanasian Creed (Quicunque vult)
works.author: Anonymous (Latin, traditionally ascribed to Athanasius)
works.summary: A Latin creed, probably from southern Gaul c. 440–540, setting out the Trinity (‘we worship one God in Trinity, and Trinity in Unity; neither confounding the persons, nor dividing the substance’) and the incarnation, with damnatory clauses.
works.significance: Used in Western liturgy and accepted by Lutheran (Book of Concord) and Anglican (Thirty-Nine Articles) confessions; not used in Orthodox liturgy.

works.title: First Apology
works.summary: Justin's defence of Christians addressed to Emperor Antoninus Pius, explaining Christian belief, the Logos, baptism and the Eucharist.
works.significance: Our earliest detailed description of Christian worship and an early statement of Logos theology.

works.title: Against Heresies (Adversus Haereses)
works.summary: Five books refuting Gnostic systems, setting out the rule of faith, apostolic succession, the fourfold Gospel and recapitulation in Christ.
works.significance: Foundational for orthodoxy, canon, tradition and the theology of salvation as recapitulation and deification.

works.title: Against Praxeas
works.summary: Tertullian's refutation of modalist monarchianism, introducing the Latin terms trinitas, persona and substantia in Trinitarian theology.
works.significance: The first systematic Latin treatise on the Trinity; its formula ‘one substance, three persons’ shaped Western theology.

works.title: On First Principles (De Principiis)
works.summary: The first Christian systematic theology: God, the Logos, the Spirit, rational creatures, free will, restoration, and the interpretation of Scripture.
works.significance: Source of the eternal generation of the Son, of three hypostases, and of later controversies over apokatastasis.

works.title: Letter to Eusebius of Nicomedia
works.summary: Arius complains of persecution by Bishop Alexander and summarises his teaching that the Son has a beginning and was made from nothing. Preserved by Theodoret (Ecclesiastical History 1.4) and Epiphanius.
works.significance: One of the few surviving texts by Arius himself.

works.title: On the Incarnation of the Word (De Incarnatione)
works.summary: Why the Word became flesh: to restore the image of God in fallen humanity, defeat death and corruption, and reveal the Father. Dated variously c. 318 or c. 335.
works.significance: Classic statement of incarnation and deification; its soteriology underlies the Nicene case against Arius.

works.title: Discourses Against the Arians (Orationes contra Arianos)
works.summary: Athanasius' main anti-Arian work: a refutation of Arius' Thalia and an exegesis of contested texts such as Proverbs 8:22, Philippians 2:9 and Hebrews 3:2.
works.significance: Set the exegetical terms of Nicene theology, including the principle of reading texts of lowliness as referring to the incarnate Son.

works.title: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
works.summary: Basil defends the doxology ‘Glory to the Father with the Son together with the Holy Spirit’, arguing for the Spirit's equal honour, and discusses unwritten apostolic traditions and the veneration of images (18.45).
works.significance: Key text for the deity of the Spirit and for the authority of unwritten tradition; cited at Nicaea II (787) for icon veneration.

works.title: Letters
works.summary: Over 360 letters, including Letter 236 and Letter 38 (sometimes attributed to Gregory of Nyssa) on the distinction of ousia and hypostasis.
works.significance: Primary source for the Cappadocian distinction between common essence and particular persons.

works.title: Theological Orations (Orations 27–31)
works.summary: Five sermons preached in Constantinople defending the Trinity against the Eunomians and the deity of the Spirit against the Pneumatomachians.
works.significance: Earned Gregory the title ‘the Theologian’; a classic of Trinitarian theology.

works.title: Oration 40: On Holy Baptism
works.summary: Gregory's Epiphany sermon on baptism, ending with an exposition of the Trinity confessed at baptism.
works.significance: Contains his celebrated description of contemplating the One and the Three.
